background.definition: Bleeding from the esophagus, stomach, or upper small bowel proximal to the ligament of Treitz is termed upper gastrointestinal bleeding (UGIB). It presents with hematemesis and/or melena, but may sometimes cause bright red hematochezia in cases with severe bleeding. See also chapter on variceal UGIB.

list.listitem: Incidence is approximately 170 cases per 100,000 adults per year.
Incidence of hospitalization for acute UGIB is 102 per 100,000 per year. It is twice as common in men as in women and increases with age.
The hospitalization rate decreased by 21% in the US from 81 to 67 cases per 100,000 from 2002-2012 suggestive of improved peptic ulcer disease treatment,hemostatic techniques and overall care
Ulcerative or erosive: peptic ulcer disease; idiopathic, drug induced, Helicobacter pylori, or stress-induced ulcer, Zollinger-Ellison syndrome (50%).
Anticoagulant use increases the risk of serious bleeding from any upper GI lesion.

Use of NSAIDs and anti-platelet agents increases the risk of upper GI hemorrhage. The ASPREE study found that in generally healthy 70 year olds the 5 year risk of GI bleeding severe enough to require hospitalization or transfusion was only 0.25% over 5 years.

Another study of 1323 patients 75 years and older with atrial fibrillation found a small increase in the risk of GI hemorrhage when they were switched from warfarin to the direct oral anticoagulant rivaroxaban. Patients were managed in a special coagulation clinic and rivaroxaban has a higher bleeding risk than apixaban, which may have influenced these results.
Traumatic or post surgical: Mallory-Weiss tear; foreign body ingestion (5%-15%).
Esophagitis: peptic, pill induced, infectious, Candida albicans, cytomegalovirus (CMV).
Duodenitis.
Stomal ulcers.

Arterial, venous, or other vascular malformations: idiopathic angiomas, Osler-Weber-Rendu syndrome, Dieulafoy's lesion, radiation-induced telangiectasia, watermelon stomach (also known as gastric antral vascular ectasia).
Benign tumors: leiomyomas, polyps, lipoma.
Malignant tumors: adenocarcinoma, lymphoma, Kaposi's sarcoma, carcinoid, metastatic tumor (5%).
Iatrogenic injuries secondary to endoscopic procedures, such as gastrostomy tube placement: rare causes of UGIB.
Miscellaneous: hemobilia, hemosuccus pancreaticus.

Peptic ulcer disease: Helicobacter pylori renders the underlying mucosa more vulnerable to acid peptic damage by disrupting the mucous layer, liberating enzymes and toxins, and adhering to the gastric epithelium. The host immune response to H. pylori also incites an inflammatory reaction that further perpetuates tissue injury.

NSAID-induced injury: due to a combination of local effects and systemic inhibition of GI mucosa cyclooxygenase (COX) activities. Risk appears to be increased when taken along with SSRI antidepressants.

Gastric acid: Factors that impair mucosal integrity like H. pylori, NSAIDs, or physiologic stress result in increased cell membrane permeability to back diffusion of hydrogen ions, resulting in intramural acidosis, cell death, and ulceration.
Mallory-Weiss tears: mucosal lacerations at gastroesophageal junction or in the cardia of the stomach, which are associated with repeated retching or vomiting.

The risk of acute variceal rebleeding in patients with cirrhosis is amplified by the presence of heparin like effect and association of Factor VII & XIII deficiency, with increased fibrinolysis as demonstrated in a recent study despite endotherapy

list.listitem: A meta-analysis concluded that primary ulcer prophylaxis with antisecretory agents such as H2 receptor antagonists or preferably proton pump inhibitors decreases the risk of stress-related mucosal damage and UGIB in high-risk patients (>4% bleeding risk). In an RCT of 1653 high-risk ICU patients randomized to pantoprazole 40 mg or placebo, there was less bleeding (2.5% vs 4.2%, NNT = 59) but no effect on mortality. B

Guidelines from the Society for Critical Care Medicine (2024) recommend that critically ill patients with risk factors for stress-related GI bleed receive a low-dose proton pump inhibitor or H2 receptor antagonist as prophylaxis. Risk factors include coagulopathy, shock, and chronic liver disease. The medication should be discontinued when the patient is discharged from the ICU. B

A study randomized 4825 adults on mechanical ventiilation to pantoprazole 40 mg daily or placebo. The clinically important UGI bleeding occurred less frequently in the pantoprazole group (1.0% vs 3.5%; hazard ratio [HR] 0.30; 95% CI 0.19 - 0.47). There was no difference in mortality or ventilator associated pneumonia. B

An RCT of patients with a previous peptic ulcer who were restarted on aspirin found a non-significant trend favoring a PPI over a H2 receptor antagonist (0.7% vs 3.1% recurrent bleeding). In an RCT of patients infected with H. pylori, omeprazole alone reduces NSAID-induced risk of rebleeding more than eradication of H. pylori (NNT = 7). A
For patients taking dual anti-platelet therapy, proton pump inhibitors reduce the likelihood of GI events (1.2% vs 3.1%, NNT = 53). A
Patients with peptic ulcer disease should be tested and treated for H. pylori—eradication reduces the long-term rate of rebleeding compared with no treatment (NNT = 7-20). A

All patients with functional dyspepsia should be evaluated for the presence of helicobacter pylori (HP) using a stool or breath test, and if the results are abnormal the patient should be treated to eradicate HP. A recent meta-analysis confirms that eradication not only reduces the risk of ulcer but is also an effective strategy in the management of functional dyspepsia( relative risk [RR] = 0.91; 95% CI 0.88 - 0.94; [NNT] = 14).
UGIB commonly presents with hematemesis (vomiting of blood or coffee-grounds emesis), and/or melena (black tarry stool), with or without. hemodynamic compromise. C
Endoscopy is the recommended initial study for diagnosis and treatment of UGIB. A
Patients with peptic ulcer disease should be tested and treated for H. pylori. A

Differential.Differential_Name: Peptic ulcer disease: drug induced, eg, by NSAIDs, alcohol
Differential.Differential_Features: History of alcohol binge or NSAID use or previous history of gastric or duodenal ulcer
History of cirrhosis; bleeding from esophageal varices can be massive
Typically, history of repeated retching or vomiting; most bleeding episodes are self-limited
Associated with chronic renal insufficiency or failure, and bleeding facilitated by acquired Von Willebrands's disease
History of weight loss and anemia
Patients are typically men with multiple comorbidities that include cardiovascular disease and chronic renal failure

list.listitem: Upper GI bleeding (UGIB) commonly presents with hematemesis (vomiting of blood or coffee-grounds emesis), and/or melena (black tarry stool), with or without hemodynamic compromise.

A nasogastric tube lavage that yields blood or coffee-grounds-like material makes a UGI source very likely. However, lavage may not be positive if bleeding has ceased or arises beyond a closed pylorus. The presence of bilious fluid indicates that the pylorus is open; if lavage is negative and bilious fluid is present, active UGIB distal to the pylorus is very unlikely.
Hematechezia may occur in patients with extremely brisk UGIB.

Important elements of the history include the use of aspirin and other NSAIDs or alcohol, history of liver disease or variceal bleeding, history of ulcers, weight loss, dysphagia, heartburn, abdominal aortic aneurysm (AAA), and/or abdominal aortic vascular graft. A history of an AAA or graft increases concern regarding an aortoenteric fistula and may require a CT scan for evaluation.

Upper panendoscopy is the diagnostic modality of choice for acute UGIB. Endoscopy is sensitive and specific for locating and identifying bleeding lesions in the upper GI tract. Endoscopy in patients with UGIB is also effective in treating most causes of UGIB and is associated with a reduction in blood transfusion requirement and length of intensive care unit and total hospital stay. Testing for H. pylori infection should be done.
Preprocedure erythromycin improves mucosal visibility.A
Early endoscopy (within 24 hours of hospital admission) has a greater impact than a later endoscopy on length of hospital stay and requirement for blood transfusion.

Obtain laboratory tests such as CBC, platelet count, and coagulation profile early in evaluation of a patient with UGIB. Elevated BUN/Cr ratio greater than 36 is very specific but not sensitive for UGI source. These data are important in the overall assessment of the patient and in subsequent follow-up.

UGI barium studies are contraindicated in acute GI bleed workup because they can interfere with future endocopy, angiography, or surgery. If gastric or duodenal ulcer is identified at the time of endoscopy, then H. pylori should be tested and if present eradicated.
Other diagnostic tests include selective angiography and tagged RBC scan, both of which can detect active bleeding. Capsule endoscopy is potentially useful for identifying small bowel bleeding.

The Blatchford score was found to be more sensitive than the Rockall score in risk scoring to predict need for clinical intervention for patients with nonvariceal UGIB and is recommended by 2019 guidelines for initial assessment. Another study compared the Blatchford score to the AIMS65 score and found that the former was superior.A direct comparison in 3012 patients at 6 large hospitals found that the Glasgow Blatchford score was most accurate with an AUROCC of 0.86 compared to 0.70 or less for other scores. A score ≤1 was the best threshold to predict survival without intervention.

Previously no scores were available to predict the risk of small bowel rebleeding after an initial small bowel capsule endoscopy.This led to the development of the RHEMITT score. Patients with occult gastrointestinal bleeding undergo small bowel capsule endoscopy, but often present with recurrent bleeding or anemia. The RHEMITT score was recently validated through a study at U.S tertiary referral center thus, confirming acceptable performance for predicting rebleeding

A novel bleeding risk score designed for elderly patients accurately predicted risk of major bleeding. Points are assigned as follows. A score of 2 or greater had the best accuracy (LR+ 1.4, LR- 0.4). This was better than other risk scores in the study population: Age 85 to 95: 1 point; Age > 95: 2 points eGFR 30 to 50: 1 point; eGFR < 30: 2 points Hemoglobin < 11 g/dl: 2 points Albumin < 35 g/L: 1 point Amiodarone use: 1 point
See algorithm in .

Endoscopy within 24 hours for patients with UGIB is the modality of choice in diagnosing and treating most causes of UGIB and is associated with a reduction in blood transfusion requirements and length of stay in intensive care unit and total hospital stay.
The source of bleeding is identified in 95% of cases, and endoscopic treatment is effective in 80% to 90% of patients.

Pretreatment with intravenous omeprazole (80 mg bolus followed by 8 mg/h) reduces the need to endoscopic treatment (NNT = 11) and increases likelihood of hospital discharge in less than 3 days (NNT = 9).
The initial management of patients with UGIB is assessment and stabilization. C
Proton pump inhibitors are recommended for patients with bleeding caused by actual or suspected peptic ulcers. A
Treatment of H. pylori infection is more effective than antisecretory noneradicating therapy in preventing recurrent bleeding from peptic ulcer disease. A
Endoscopic therapy is indicated within 24 hours for most patients; pretreatment with a PPI reduces rebleeding risk and the need for endoscopic hemostasis.A

Guidelines recommend against the use of idarucizumab (if taking dabigatran), andexanet alfa (if taking rivaroxaban or apixaban), and vitamin K or fresh frozen plasma (if taking warfarin) for patients presenting with an acute GI hemorrhage. B

Proton pump inhibitors (PPIs) will improve short-term outcomes in patients presenting with bleeding gastric or duodenal ulcers. A study comparing IV omeprazole with IV omeprazole plus endoscopy therapy in patients with UGIB and a nonbleeding visible vessel or adherent clot showed that patients who received combination therapy had fewer episodes of recurrent bleeding and had lower blood transfusion requirements (NNT = 10 for combined therapy vs proton pump inhibitor alone). Omeprazole reduces morbidity in bleeding peptic ulcer disease. There are no data to support use of H2 receptor antagonists in acute GI bleeds. This intervention has not been shown to decrease transfusion or rebleeding rates.

A Cochrane review of 6 RCTs with 2223 patients concluded that pretreatment with a PPI prior to upper endoscopy for patients with upper GI bleeding reduces the risk of rebleeding and the need for endoscopic hemostatic treatment, but does not appear to affect the need for surgery or mortality.

2019 guidelines recommend that patients with bleeding ulcers and high-risk stigmata receive high-dose PPI for 3 days, then twice daily orally for two weeks, then once daily with the overall duration based on the underlying lesion being treated and patient response.

A meta-analysis found 10 RCTs showing that intermittent PPI therapy was non-inferior to continuous PPI infusion. Intermittent regimens ranged from pantoprazole 40 mg orally every 12 hours to pantoprazole 80 mg IV once followed by 40 mg IV every 6 hours.

Over the years, proton pump inhibitors (PPIs) have been the mainstay of treatment for erosive esophagitis which accounts for 11% of cases of upper gastrointestinal bleed. A randomized control trial compared Vonoprazan, a potassium-competitive acid blocker with lansoprazole revealing that Vonoprazan was noninferior and superior to the PPI lansoprazole in healing and maintenance of healing of erosive esophagitis. This benefit was seen predominantly in more severe erosive esophagitis.

Tranexamic acid is an anti-fibrolytic that has been studied in patients with upper gastrointestinal bleeding. A Cochrane review found 8 trials with a total of 1701 participants, mostly randomized to tranexamic acid or placebo (some trials included an anti-acid drug arm as well). They found a significant reduction in mortality (RR 0.60; 95% CI 0.42-0.87) and a borderline reduction in rebleeding, but no increase in thromboembolic complications. However, the benefit was not seen when limiting the analysis to studies with adequately follow-up.

A large 2021 RCT randomized 12,009 patients at 164 centers worldwide with GI bleeding (89% upper) to tranexamic acid (1 gm loading dose followed by 3 gm maintenance dose over 24 hours) or matching placebo. There was no difference in the likelihood of death at 5 days (3.7% tranexamic acid vs 3.8% placebo). There was also no difference in arterial thromboembolic events, but a small increase was seen in the risk of venous thromboembolism (0.8% vs 0.4%, RR 1.9, 95% CI 1.1-3.0).
Patients with recurrent ulcer-related bleeding can be safely managed with repeat endoscopy. Failure rates of endoscopic injection to control bleeding can be predicted using a clinical rule.

Somatostatin or octreotide was associated with a reduction in continued bleeding or rebleeding in a recent meta-analysis of 14 trials (NNT = 5). Among seven investigator-blinded trials, the NNT was 11 in the same meta-analysis. However, pantoprozole was shown to be more effective than somatostatin for peptic ulcer rebleeding.

IV erythromycin 30 to 90 minutes before esophagogastroduodenoscopy (EGD) promotes gastric motility and emptying of gastric contents and, therefore, can significantly improve visualization. Also, pretreatment with omeprazole before endoscopy reduces bleeding.

Treatment of H. pylori infection is more effective than antisecretory noneradicating therapy in preventing recurrent bleeding from peptic ulcer disease. Three highly effective regimens include 7 to 14 days of PPI + amoxicillin + clarithromycin + metronidazole, 10 to 14 days of PPI + amoxicillin + clarithromycin + probiotics, and 14 days of PPI + levofloxacin + another antibiotic.
Give prophylactic antibiotics to patients with cirrhosis, preferably before endoscopy, to reduce infectious complications.

Among 921 patients with an acute upper GI bleed, a restrictive transfusion strategy using a hemoglobin transfusion threshold of less than 7 g/dL (with a post transfusion hemoglobin goal of 7-9 g/dL) compared to a liberal transfusion strategy using a transfusion threshold of 9 g/dL (with a post transfusion hemoglobin goal of 9-11 g/dL) results in decreased 45-day mortality rates (5% vs 9%), shorter hospital stays 9.6 vs 11.5 days), and decreased rates of further bleeding (10% vs 16%) fewer adverse events (40% vs 48%) in patients with acute upper gastrointestinal bleeding.

listitem.strong: Management in patients taking oral anticoagulants

list.listitem: For patients taking dabigatran, idarucizumab reverses anticoagulation.

For patients taking a factor Xa inhibitor such as apixaban, andexanet alfa may improve hemostasis.. The final study on treatment with andexanet alfa demonstrated reduced anti-FXa activity and was associated with excellent hemostatic efficacy in 80% of patients [95% CI, 75-84] with major bleeding associated with the use of FXa inhibitors

However, 2022 guidelines from the American College of Gastroenterology and Canadian Association of Gastroenterology (ACT/CAG) recommend against the use of idarucizumab (if taking dabigatran) and andexanet alfa (if taking rivaroxaban or apixaban) for patients presenting with an acute GI hemorrhage. The guidelines also recommend against the use of fresh frozen plasma or vitamin K for patients taking a vitamin K antagonist such as warfarin. They could not reach a recommendation for or against use of prothrombin complex concentrate (PCC) for patients taking a vitamin K antagonist. They also recommend against the use of PCC for patients taking a direct oral anticoagulant. Most of these recommendations were based on poor or very poor quality evidence.

For patients taking an antiplatelet agent, the 2022 ACG/CAG guidelines recommend against platelet transfusions. They also recommend against holding aspirin in patients who are taking it for secondary cardiovascular prevention (i.e. those with a previous cardiac event or stroke). If aspirin was held, it should be resumed on the day that hemostasis is endoscopically confirmed.

Surgery is indicated in patients with shock associated with recurrent hemorrhage, hemodynamic instability despite vigorous resuscitation (>3 U of blood transfusion), or continued slow bleeding requiring more than 3 U of blood per day.

Endoscopic therapy is indicated within 24 hours for most patients with active bleeding or spurting arterial vessels or visible vessels that are nonbleeding. Clean based ulcers are at very low risk for rebleeding. Available endoscopic treatment modalities include injection, cautery, and mechanical therapy. There is no clear superiority among the different modalities. Preprocedure erythromycin improves mucosal visibility.

A study randomized 516 patients to urgent endoscopy within 6 hours versus endoscopy within 24 hours or the next morning and found no benefit of urgent endoscopy in terms of mortality or further rebleeding.

A meta-analysis identified 9 RCTs with 833 patients comparing endoscopic with conservative therapy in patients with bleeding peptic ulcer and an adherent clot. They found lower rates of overall rebleeding (OR 0.41, 95% CI 0.22-0.79) and mortality (OR 0.47 95% CI 0.23-0.95) with endoscopic therapy.
2019 guidelines recommend thermocoagulation and sclerosant injection, with clips as an option, in patients with high-risk stigmata. Hemostatic powder is not recommended as sole treatment.

The most commonly studied hemostatic powder is TC-325 which is a silica based biologically inert powder creating a mechanical barrier over a bleeding site. The largest RCT compared TC-325 with conventional endoscopy included 224 patients with non variceal upper gastrointestinal bleed and the outcome of this study indicated TC-325 was noninferior to conventional endoscopy in securing hemostasis(90.1% vs 81.4% OR: 8.7 1-sided 95% CI:0.95), 30-day recurrent bleeding(8.1vs 8.8% OR:0.91 95% CI: 0.37-2.22) or 30-day mortality(12.6% vs 12.4% OR: 1.02 95%CI 0.46-2.25 )

In a meta-analysis to evaluate the efficacy of topical hemostatic agent in malignacy associated GI bleed, TC-325 have been shown to be effective in achieving primary hemostatsis in malignant hemorrhagic lesion of the gastrointestinal tract in 94.1% cases with (95% confidence interval [CI], 91.5-96.0)

A multi-site RCT of 66 patients with rebleeding of a peptic ulcer following initial successful hemostasis compared over-the-scope clips with usual care (largely through the scope clip). The rate of persistent bleeding (6.0% vs 42.4%, p = 0.001, NNT = 3) was lower in the over the scope clip group, as was the likliheood of any further bleeding (15.2% vs 57.6%, p = 0.001, NNT = 3). There was no difference in mortality or need for surgery.However in a recent multicenter open labeled RCT, comparing efficacy of over- the -scope clips to standard endoscopic therapy in primary treatment of patients with peptic ulcer bleeding that are of size ≥1.5 cm. The routine use of over- the -scope clips as primary haemostasis in these large bleeding peptic ulcers was not associated with a significant decrease in 30-day rebleeding despite successful primary hemostasis.Management options for patients who fail to stop bleeding with endoscopic treatment include repeat endoscopy, emergency surgery, and transcatheter arteriography followed by transcatheter intervention (usually embolization). A small RCT compared transcatheter arterial embolization in high risk patients with peptic ulcer bleeding vs standard therapy, and found a trend toward fewer rebleeds with intervention (2 vs 8, p = 0.1).
Surgery and transcatheter arteriography/intervention are both equally effective in treating patients with acute nonvariceal UGIB that fails to respond to endoscopic treatment.

In patients with a perforated peptic ulcer, a Cochrane review of three RCTs noted no statistically significant differences between laparoscopic and open surgery. There was a trend toward fewer septic abdominal complications and pulmonary complications.

Among 921 patients with an acute upper GI bleed, a restrictive transfusion strategy using a hemoglobin transfusion threshold of less than 7 g/dL (with a post transfusion hemoglobin goal of 7-9 g/dL) compared to a liberal transfusion strategy using a transfusion threshold of 9 g/dL (with a post transfusion hemoglobin goal of 9-11 g/dL) results in decreased 45-day mortality rates (5% vs 9%), shorter hospital stays 9.6 vs 11.5 days), and decreased rates of further bleeding (10% vs 16%) fewer adverse events (40% vs 48%) in patients with acute upper gastrointestinal bleeding.
Guidelines (2019) recommend a threshold for transfusion of 8 g/dl, and a higher threshold for patients with underlying cardiovascular disease.
Many patients with UGIB can be managed as outpatients, if they are shown to be low risk.

High-risk patients are those with hematemesis, hemodynamic instability, coagulopathy, renal failure, older age, and multiple comorbidities. These patients require more intensive monitoring. A clinical rule can predict the need for intervention in patients with GI bleed.
Admit to the ICU all patients with hemodynamic instability or active bleeding for resuscitation and close observation.

Complications that could arise before endoscopy include aspiration, hypoventilation, and hypotension; manage these with careful airway management or endotracheal intubation. Manage hypotension with aggressive resuscitation including transfusion of packed RBCs.
Complications of endoscopic hemostasis therapy include perforation and precipitation (or worsening) of bleeding, and may require surgery.
The probability of persistent bleeding after injection can be predicted by clinical decision rules such as the Blatchford and Rockall scores. A

Predictors of rebleeding include older age; shock, hemodynamic instability, or orthostasis; comorbid diseases; specific endoscopic findings (eg, malignancy); use of anticoagulant or coagulopathy; or presence of a high-risk lesion (arterial bleeding) nonvisible vessel, or clot. A

Untreated peptic ulcers have a wide variation in natural history. Some heal spontaneously, but they are associated with a high rate of recurrence. Studies have shown a 50% to 80% recurrence rate within 6 to 12 months of initial healing, although relapses are not always symptomatic.

Predictors of rebleeding include older age; shock, hemodynamic instability or orthostasis; comorbid diseases; specific endoscopic findings (eg, malignancy); use of anticoagulant or coagulopathy; or presence of a high-risk lesion (arterial bleeding) nonvisible vessel, or clot. The probability of persistent bleeding after injection can be predicted by a clinical decision rule.

In a study that followed 1000 patients with HP eradication following peptic ulcer bleed for 3253 patient-years, the likelihood of recurrent bleeding was only 0.15% per patient-year, and only occurred in patients who took NSAIDs or were reinfected.
Proton pump inhibitors decrease rebleeding but not mortality with bleeding ulcers.
Elevated serum lactate levels on admission are associated with higher inpatient mortality rates.
A case-control study found an association of peptic ulcer disease with osteoporosis (HR 1.9), although the mechanism is unclear and unmeasured confounding may be an issue.
Routine second-look endoscopy is not recommended.
A second attempt at endoscopy therapy is generally recommended in cases of rebleeding.
Studies suggest that scheduled repeat endoscopy in high-risk patients reduces the rebleeding rate and may be cost effective in these patients.
Test patients for H. pylori infection (urea breath test or stool antigen); eradicate infection if present.
NSAID should be avoided if possible.
Smoking should be discontinued.
Excessive use of alcohol impairs ulcer healing.
PCSK9 inhibitors do not increase the risk of gastrointestinal haemorrhage with high level of evidence as shown in a recent meta- analysis in patient who require lipid lowering therapy
Patients who are elderly or have cardiovascular disease are at a high risk of acute myocardial infarction (AMI); monitor them appropriately. Consider ruling out AMI.
Transfuse high-risk patients (elderly patients or patients with much comorbidity) with packed RBCs to keep their hematocrit above 30.
